opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the intuition is pretty simple once you think about it in terms of compute rather than per-sample quality. People usually default to the biggest, strongest model to generate synthetic data, because each individual sample is better. But if you fix your sampling budget, say a fixed number of FLOPs, a smaller model lets you draw many more samples per problem. In our work on compute-matched sampling, a model like Gemma 9B versus 27B gives you roughly three times as many samples for the same cost.

More samples buys you two things. First, coverage: you solve more of the unique problems in your training set at least once, because you get more shots on goal. Second, diversity: you get more distinct correct solutions per problem, which turns out to matter a lot for fine-tuning.

The catch is that the weaker model also produces more garbage, and that's where filtering comes in. For reasoning tasks like math, you can check the final answer against ground truth and throw away everything that's wrong. So you're exploiting the smaller model's breadth while the filter cleans up its mistakes. The thing filtering doesn't fully fix is false positives, where the model gets the right answer through flawed reasoning, and those do show up somewhat more with weaker models. But empirically the gains from coverage and diversity outweigh that cost.

And we saw it hold across settings: knowledge distillation, self-improvement, and even what we called weak-to-strong improvement, where a smaller model's filtered data actually helps train a stronger model better than that stronger model's own data does at the same compute. That was a bit counterintuitive, but it really comes down to the filter letting you treat generation as a search problem. Cheap search plus a good verifier beats expensive search with fewer attempts.

r001.rationale: It explains that a weaker model generates more samples for the same compute, and filtering removes incorrect reasoning-task outputs, making its broader sample coverage useful for synthetic training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the intuition here is actually pretty simple once you think about it in terms of compute. When you're generating synthetic data, you have a fixed budget, and the question is how you spend it. A big model gives you higher-quality samples per call, but each call is expensive. A smaller model gives you lower-quality samples, but you can get way more of them for the same cost.

Now, if you had to use every sample you generated, the big model would win, because the average quality matters. But you don't have to use everything. For a lot of the domains we care about, like math or code, you have a verifier. You can check whether the final answer is correct, you can run the unit tests. So you generate a lot of candidates from the small model, throw away the ones that fail, and keep the ones that pass.

What that does is it decouples coverage from per-sample quality. The small model might only solve a given problem ten percent of the time, but if you sample it a hundred times, you'll probably find a correct solution. And because it's cheap, you can afford to do that across many more problems. So in our compute-matched comparisons, the data from the weaker model ends up covering more unique problems and having more diverse solutions, which is actually what you want for training.

The catch is false positives. A verifier that only checks the final answer will let through solutions where the reasoning is wrong but the answer happens to be right, and the weaker model produces more of those. We saw a higher false positive rate with the smaller model, and that's a real concern. But in practice, the gain from coverage and diversity outweighed that cost, and models fine-tuned on the filtered small-model data did better than ones fine-tuned on the big-model data at the same compute.

So the short version is: filtering turns a quality problem into a search problem, and small models are really good at cheap search.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a smaller, weaker model can generate many low-cost candidates in domains such as math and code, then filtering with a verifier keeps correct samples for training.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that generating a good answer consistently is a different problem from generating a good answer sometimes. A smaller model might not be reliable enough to use directly, but if you sample enough responses and have a way to identify the good ones, those responses can still be useful training data.

Filtering lets you trade off quantity for quality. If checking an answer is easier than producing it—for example, if you can run tests on generated code—you can use a relatively cheap model to generate lots of candidates and keep only the ones that pass. The limitation is that filtering can only select capabilities the model already has some probability of expressing. It can’t recover a correct answer if the model never generates one.

r001.rationale: The response explains how filtering can make a smaller, less reliable model useful for synthetic training data, but it does not communicate that this applies to reasoning domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to generate a good answer consistently and being able to generate one sometimes. A smaller model might not be reliable on every attempt, but if you sample multiple responses, some of them can still be very good. If you have a way to identify those responses—say, checking whether code passes tests—you can keep the successes and discard the failures.

So the quality of the training data doesn’t have to equal the average quality of the model generating it. Filtering lets you trade more sampling for better data, and smaller models make that sampling cheaper. The caveat is that your filter has to actually measure what you care about; otherwise, you can end up selecting answers that look good without being correct.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a smaller model can produce strong answers intermittently, and filtering can retain those successes for synthetic training data while discarding failures. It gives code tests as an example of evaluating outputs.
